title: Tenses: Choosing the Right Time Form

blocks.text: "I have seen him yesterday." Almost every Nigerian candidate has written a sentence like that, and it costs a mark every time. The verb form is fine and the vocabulary is fine — the problem is that *yesterday* is a closed door and the present perfect can only be used while the door is still open.

blocks.markdown:
**Tense** is the form a verb takes to show *when* something happens and *how* it relates to other events. English builds twelve forms from three times and four aspects.

- Times: **present**, **past**, **future**
- Aspects: **simple**, **continuous**, **perfect**, **perfect continuous**

Examiners rarely ask you to recite them. They give you a sentence containing a **time expression** and expect you to pick the form that matches it.

blocks.caption: The twelve tense forms of English

blocks.title: Let the time expression choose the tense
blocks.text: *Yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago* → simple past. *Since, for, so far, already, just, ever, never* → present perfect. *By the time ... , before ... , after ...* with two past events → past perfect. *By next December* → future perfect. *Now, at the moment, currently* → continuous.

blocks.markdown:
### Simple past against present perfect

This single distinction accounts for more lost marks than any other.

- **Simple past** — the time is finished and usually stated: *I **saw** him **yesterday**.*
- **Present perfect** — the time is unstated, or the period is still running: *I **have seen** him **twice this term**.*

So "I have seen him yesterday" is impossible, because *yesterday* is over.

### Past perfect for the earlier of two past events

When two things happened in the past, the earlier one takes the past perfect:
> By the time we **reached** the park, the last bus **had left**.

blocks.title: Working out the tense of a reported statement
blocks.prompt: Report this statement: Musa said, "I am writing my project report."

steps.text: Check the tense of the reporting verb. It is *said*, which is past, so the reported words must shift one step back.
Identify the tense of the original words. *Am writing* is present continuous.
Shift it one step back. Present continuous becomes past continuous: *was writing*.
Adjust the pronouns to the reporter's point of view. *I* becomes *he* and *my* becomes *his*.
Insert *that* and assemble the sentence: 'Musa said that he was writing his project report.'
Check any time and place words. Had the original contained *today*, it would become *that day*; *here* would become *there*.

blocks.answer: Musa said that he was writing his project report.

rows: simple past — if I had money
would + verb — I would buy it
past perfect — if I had studied
would have + participle — I would have passed
blocks.caption: The three conditional patterns, which are really tense patterns in disguise

blocks.title: Never put *will* in the *if* clause
blocks.text: "If it will rain, we will stay indoors" is wrong. Write "If it **rains**, we will stay indoors." The same applies to *would*: the second conditional is "If I **had** money, I would buy it", never "If I would have money".

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: In the essay paper, choose your tense in the first sentence and hold it. A narrative essay normally runs in the simple past; an argumentative essay normally runs in the simple present. Random shifts between the two are treated as grammatical errors even when each sentence is correct on its own.

points: English has twelve tense forms built from three times and four aspects.
The time expression in the sentence usually decides which tense is required.
The simple past goes with finished stated time; the present perfect goes with unstated or open time.
The past perfect marks the earlier of two past events.
After a past reporting verb, the reported verb shifts one step back.
Never use *will* or *would* inside the *if* clause of a conditional sentence.
Keep one tense throughout a passage unless the meaning genuinely changes.
